title: Newborns Sticking Out Their Tongues
text:
In the 1970s, many psychologists followed Jean Piaget in believing that babies could not imitate facial expressions until near the end of their first year. Imitating a face is a hard problem: a baby can see the adult's face but cannot see its own, so it would have to link a seen movement with a felt one.

Andrew Meltzoff and M. Keith Moore at the University of Washington tested this with infants only 12 to 21 days old. An adult sat facing the baby and, in turn, stuck out his tongue, opened his mouth wide, pushed out his lips and slowly moved his fingers. The babies' faces were videotaped, and coders who did not know which gesture the adult had just made judged what each baby was doing.

The infants seemed to match the gestures more often than chance would predict: more tongue protrusion after seeing tongue protrusion, more mouth opening after seeing mouth opening. Meltzoff and Moore published the result in Science in 1977 and later reported similar findings with newborns only hours old.

The claim was exciting because it suggested that babies arrive ready to connect with other people, treating faces as something like their own from the very start.
lesson: Even the youngest babies are watching faces closely. Face-to-face play with an infant is not idle; it is the start of a conversation.
source: Meltzoff, A. N., and Moore, M. K. (1977). Imitation of facial and manual gestures by human neonates. Science, 198(4312), 75-78.
caveat: The finding is disputed: a large 2016 longitudinal study by Oostenbroek and colleagues found no reliable newborn imitation, though Meltzoff and others contest its methods.
